newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico insists wants speedy global landmines ban.
newsitem.headline: Mexico insists wants speedy global landmines ban.

text.p: Mexico wants a global landmine ban but believes a U.N.-backed disarmament forum in Geneva is not the best or fastest way to achieve that goal, Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria said on Thursday.
He was speaking after Mexico blocked a Western attempt to launch negotiations on a global landmine ban at the Geneva Conference on Disarmament, which has been discussing nuclear disarmament.

"Mexico is a champion of a total landmine ban. In Mexico there are no mines and we don't produce mines. We don't have a mines industry in Mexico and mines are not used for any purpose and will never be used," Gurria told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Some Western diplomats expressed confusion and disappointment over the veto but Gurria said Mexico had objected because it preferred to wipe out mines via a speedier negotiating process in a separate body, the Ottawa Process.

"The problem we have is that the introduction of the (mines) topic in the disarmament conference, we believe, will guarantee that the process will be very long and very slow and we want to give priority to the Ottawa forum," he said.
Some 50 countries have joined the Ottawa process and the group hopes to have a draft global treaty banning landmines ready for signing at the end of the year, Gurria added.
However, China and Russia -- major producers and users of landmines -- are not taking part in the Ottawa forum. Some diplomats say this means a viable, universal ban could only be clinched in Geneva.
Gurria said the Ottawa countries preferred to agree quickly on a draft treaty and then pressure other nations to join in and sign.
Nonetheless Mexico would not rule out discussing a landmine ban in Geneva if the negotiating mandate were changed, even though it believed the Ottawa process offered a better solution, Gurria added.

Gurria flatly denied a suggestion by an unnamed Western diplomat in the confusion after the Geneva vote that Mexico might have wanted to "keep mines for possible use in Chiapas", a southern state which saw an Indian uprising in 1994.
Gurria said this was totally false.

"In Chiapas there are no mines, in Mexico there are no mines, they are not produced or used here," he said. "This has nothing to do with internal issues. This is part of our foreign policy which has been invariable (in favour of a rapid total landmine ban)".

Independent observers have not reported seeing landmines in Chiapas. Fighting between the Zapatista rebels and the Mexican army lasted several weeks in 1994 but since then there have been no further clashes.
The two sides were negotiating a peace treaty last year, though talks are currently stalled over differing interpretations of earlier government promises.
